source_text:
σημαινέτω μὲν οὖν τι καὶ ὑψηλότερον ἡ κάμηλος διὰ στενῆς ὁδοῦ καὶ τεθλιμμένης φθάνουσα τὸν πλούσιον, ὅπερ ἐν τῇ περὶ ἀρχῶν καὶ θεολογίας ἐξηγήσει μυστήριον τοῦ σωτῆρος ὑπάρχει μαθεῖν·
οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ τό γε φαινόμενον πρῶτον καὶ δι᾿ ὃ λέλεκται τῆς παραβολῆς παρεχέσθω. διδασκέτω τοὺς εὐποροῦντας ὡς οὐκ ἀμελητέον τῆς ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίας ὡς ἤδη προκατεγνωσμένους οὐδὲ καταποντιστέον αὖ πάλιν τὸν πλοῦτον οὐδὲ καταδικαστέον ὡς τῆς ζωῆς ἐπίβουλον καὶ πολέμιον, ἀλλὰ μαθητέον τίνα τρόπον καὶ πῶς πλούτῳ χρηστέον καὶ τὴν ζωὴν κτητέον. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ οὔτε ἐκ παντὸς ἀπόλλυταί τις, ὅτι πλουτεῖ δεδιώς, οὔτε ἐκ παντὸς σῴζεται θαρρῶν καὶ πιστεύων ὡς σωθήσεται, φέρε σκεπτέον ἥντινα τὴν ἐλπίδα αὐτοῖς ὁ σωτὴρ ὑπογράφει καὶ πῶς ἂν τὸ μὲν ἀνέλπιστον ἐχέγγυον γένοιτο, τὸ δὲ ἐλπισθὲν εἰς κτῆσιν ἀφίκοιτο.
Φησὶν οὖν ὁ διδάσκαλος, τίς ἡ μεγίστη τῶν ἐντολῶν ἠρωτημένος· »ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς δυνάμεώς σου«, ταύτης μείζω μηδεμίαν ἐντολὴν εἶναι, καὶ μάλα εἰκότως, καὶ γὰρ καὶ περὶ τοῦ πρώτου καὶ περὶ τοῦ μεγίστου παρήγγελται. αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν, δι᾿ οὗ καὶ γέγονε καὶ ἔστι τὰ πάντα καὶ εἰς ὃν τὰ σῳζόμενα πάλιν ἐπανέρχεται. ὑπὸ τούτου τοίνυν προαγαπηθέντας καὶ τοῦ γενέσθαι τυχόντας οὐχ ὅσιον ἄλλο τι πρεσβύτερον ἄγειν καὶ τιμιώτερον, ἐκτίνοντας μόνην τὴν χάριν ταύτην μικρὰν ἐπὶ μεγίστοις, ἄλλο δὲ μηδοτιοῦν ἔχοντας ἀνενδεεῖ καὶ τελείῳ θεῷ πρὸς ἀμοιβὴν ἐπινοῆσαι, αὐτῷ δὲ τῷ ἀγαπᾶν τὸν πατέρα εἰς οἰκείαν ἰσχὺν καὶ δύναμιν ἀφθαρσίαν κομιζομένους, ὅσον γὰρ ἀγαπᾷ τις θεόν, τοσούτῳ καὶ πλέον ἐνδοτέρω τοῦ θεοῦ παραδύεται.
thought_title: The camel's deeper meaning and the right use of wealth
orientation: Clement is interpreting Jesus' saying about the camel and the needle's eye, first noting its hidden theological meaning, then drawing out its plain lesson for the rich.
pass_a_gloss: Let the camel then signify something also higher, passing through a narrow and constricted way ahead of the rich person, which mystery of the Savior it is possible to learn in the exposition concerning first principles and theology. But nevertheless let the apparent meaning first, and the reason for which the parable has been spoken, be supplied. Let it teach those who are well off that they must not neglect their own salvation as if already condemned beforehand, nor again must wealth be sunk in the sea, nor must it be condemned as a plotter and enemy of life, but they must learn in what manner and how wealth is to be used and life is to be acquired. For since neither does someone perish in every case because he is rich and afraid, nor is someone saved in every case because he is confident and believes that he will be saved, come, let us consider what hope the Savior sketches out for them and how the hopeless thing might become secure and the hoped-for thing might arrive at possession. The teacher then, when asked what is the greatest of the commandments, says: 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your strength,' that no commandment is greater than this, and very reasonably, for indeed it has been commanded concerning the first and greatest thing, God our Father himself, through whom all things have come to be and are, and to whom the things being saved return again. Therefore those who have been loved beforehand by him and have obtained existence, it is not holy to lead any other thing as older and more honored, paying back this grace alone, small in return for the greatest things, and having nothing else at all to devise as recompense to a God who is without need and perfect, but by loving the Father itself they receive incorruption into their own strength and power. For as much as someone loves God, by so much also does he slip further inside God.

lemmas.gloss: let it be supplied, let it be presented
must not be sunk in the sea

choices.english: passing ahead of the rich person
choices.why: φθάνω with accusative means to overtake or outstrip; the camel reaches the narrow way before the rich person, preserving the paradox of the Gospel image

choices.english: must not be sunk in the sea
choices.why: The verb καταποντίζω specifically means to plunge or sink into the sea; Clement is rejecting the idea that wealth must be destroyed or thrown away
ἐπίβουλος means one who plots against or schemes, and πολέμιος means hostile enemy; both are personifications of wealth as an active threat to life
ἐχέγγυος means guaranteed, reliable, or secure; Clement asks how the hopeless case can become a sure pledge
παραδύομαι means to slip in or penetrate alongside; the comparative πλέον ἐνδοτέρω intensifies the inward movement toward God

bible_refs.note: ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς δυνάμεώς σου

pass_b_english: Let the camel, then, also signify something higher as it reaches the rich person through the narrow and constricted way—a mystery of the Savior that can be learned in the exposition of first principles and theology. But for now, let the first and obvious meaning, the reason the parable was spoken, be presented. Let it teach those who have means that they must not neglect their own salvation as if they were already condemned in advance, nor must wealth be sunk in the sea again, nor condemned as a plotter and enemy of life. Instead, they must learn in what manner and how wealth must be used and life must be acquired. For since no one is destroyed simply because he is rich and afraid, and no one is saved simply because he is confident and believes he will be saved, come, let us consider what hope the Savior sketches out for them, and how what is hopeless might become secure, and what is hoped for might arrive at possession.

So the Teacher, when asked which is the greatest of the commandments, says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5 (cf. Mark 12:30)). He says that no commandment is greater than this, and very rightly so, for it was commanded concerning the first and greatest reality—God our Father himself, through whom all things came to be and exist, and to whom all that are saved return again. Since we were first loved by him and received our very coming into being, it is not holy to hold anything else as older or more precious than him. We repay this one small favor for the greatest gifts, and we have nothing at all to devise as recompense for a God who lacks nothing and is perfect. But by the very act of loving the Father, we receive incorruption as our own strength and power. For as much as someone loves God, by that much he slips further inside God.

problems.quote: passes ahead of the rich person
problems.why: φθάνουσα means 'reaching, attaining, arriving at', not 'passes ahead of'. The camel reaches/arrives at the rich person (or the rich person reaches through), not passes ahead of him.
problems.fix: reaching the rich person, or as the rich person reaches through
problems.ruling: φθάνουσα = reaches/arrives, not passes ahead; English misstates camel's relation to the rich person.

problems.source_quote: »ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς δυνάμεώς σου«
problems.why: The quotation matches Mark 12:30 (and parallels: Matt 22:37, Luke 10:27). However, Clement's context is about the greatest commandment, which appears in all three Synoptics. Mark 12:30 has 'ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σου...καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου...καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου...καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου'—four parts. Clement's text has only two parts: 'ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς δυνάμεώς σου'. This actually matches more closely with Luke 10:27 (which has 'ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σου...καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ ψυχῇ σου...καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ ἰσχύϊ σου...καὶ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ διανοίᾳ σου') or is an abbreviated form. But Mark 12:30 specifically includes 'heart' and 'mind'. The citation 'Mark 12:30' is not clearly wrong since Clement may be abbreviating, but the verse reference is not precise. However, the brief says 'Clement quotes the Gospels, especially Mark, and also Matthew and Luke.' The quotation as given in Clement does not exactly match Mark 12:30's full form. But Clement often abbreviates. Is this a 'wrong scripture'? The English cites Mark 12:30, but Clement's text has only two clauses where Mark has four. This is a shortened quotation, not necessarily wrong. Yet if we're strict: Mark 12:30 reads 'ἀγαπήσεις...ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς διανοίας σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου'. Clement has 'ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς σου καὶ ἐξ ὅλης τῆς δυνάμεώς σου'. This is NOT Mark 12:30. It is closer to an abbreviated Deut 6:5 or mixed form. The citation is misleading.
problems.ruling: Citation given as Mark 12:30 but Greek quote omits heart and mind, not a verbatim Mark passage.

problems.source_quote: αὐτῷ δὲ τῷ ἀγαπᾶν τὸν πατέρα
problems.why: αὐτῷ δὲ τῷ ἀγαπᾶν = 'but by the very act of loving' (dat. of means with articular infinitive). 'itself' is wrong—αὐτῷ here is not 'itself' but intensive with the articular infinitive: 'by loving itself' i.e. 'by the very act of loving'. 'The Father itself' is confusing and ungrammatical in English (the Father is masculine, not neuter). Should be 'by the very act of loving the Father' or 'by loving the Father itself' if 'itself' modifies the act. As written, 'the Father itself' sounds like the Father is an 'it'.
problems.fix: by the very act of loving the Father
problems.ruling: αὐτῷ τῷ ἀγαπᾶν = by the very act of loving; 'the Father itself' misreads αὐτῷ.

edits.old: passes ahead of the rich person

edits.new: by the very act of loving the Father

fixed: φθάνουσα means 'reaching, attaining', not 'passes ahead of'; changed to 'reaches the rich person'.
Clement's quotation has only two clauses, matching Deuteronomy 6:5 rather than the four-part Mark 12:30; changed citation.
αὐτῷ δὲ τῷ ἀγαπᾶν is an intensive with the articular infinitive, meaning 'by the very act of loving'; changed to avoid 'the Father itself'.

last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ διδάσκαλος, τίς ἡ μεγίστη τῶν ἐντολῶν ἠρωτημένος
last_rejected.why: Clement attributes this to Jesus 'the Teacher' answering a question, which matches Mark 12:30 (parallel to Matthew 22:37, Luke 10:27). The primary citation should be Mark 12:30, not Deuteronomy 6:5 with Mark as cf.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek quotes Deut 6:5; Mark is only a cross‑reference, not a mis‑citation

last_rejected.quote: as it reaches the rich person
last_rejected.why: Greek says the camel crushes/overcomes the rich man, not merely reaches him; agency and sense are altered.
last_rejected.fix: as it overcomes the rich person
last_rejected.ruling: φθάνω means 'reach, arrive at' (LSJ); 'reaches' is correct. 'Crushes' is unattested.
